title: The Permission Slip
lead: An eight-year-old from the school ship Wintermere walks onto your bridge with a permission slip in crayon. She wants you to sign it, because the singing people say they can give back her mum's letters, but only if a grown-up says it's okay.
anyone: An eight-year-old from the school ship Wintermere has been going around with a permission slip in crayon. She wants a grown-up to sign it, because the singing people say they can give back her mum's letters.

gm.truth: A teacher on the Wintermere, Davit Pereira, had his class write letters to the people they'd lost, as a grief exercise. Some of the kids built a crystal radio in science club and started reading the letters out at night. Three weeks ago something answered. It's gentle, and it uses the pet names their parents used. Fourteen children now talk to it, and they're the calmest kids on the ship. Everything it says is something that parent really said in life. It never says anything new, and one or two of the children have started to notice. It's what's left of their parents in the song, doing what those parents would have done, as well as it can. It's asking for permission because Ife Daramola's mother never let her do anything without asking a grown-up, and it remembers. What it's offering is real: the mothers' own letters, never sent. Accepting means a long burst of data from the song. This time, it's not an attack. But an open channel is an open channel, and the Cantor is now turning to look, very gently. Ife's real question comes later, in private: "If the silver lady has my mum's face, is she a little bit my mum?"
beats: Ife on the bridge with her slip. Naomi Cass brought her. Everyone is very still. Pell has gone white, and Lira's skin goes a color nobody has seen.
The classroom: a radio made of spare wire and a lunch tin, and fourteen calm children who aren't at all afraid. Mr. Pereira didn't know, and he's devastated. The kids show the captain how it works.

The other end of the line. The captain can listen. It calls them by their first name and asks if they've eaten. Tarrow wants the radio destroyed and the kids questioned. Seven wants the radio, very badly.
Iven or Lira reports a faint shift in something far away.
Ife asks again, and wants to know why the captain is taking so long. Then she asks the other question.
routes: Build it properly: engineering and hacking for a filter that lets words in and nothing out, or moving the radio far from the fleet on a drone. It might work.

Listen and learn: attunement through the lunch tin, and science or lore on what's being said. The only real conversation anyone has had with the Choir is running through a class of eight-year-olds. Someone is going to suggest using it, and the captain has to decide if it can be them.

End it: leadership or intimidation. Take the radio and explain to fourteen children why. If the captain wants a kind lie, deception will do it, and Naomi offers to forge the replies: she has practice.
Say yes: sign the slip, with Ife watching. Whatever comes through comes through.
checks: persuasion:moderate to get the children to trust you with the radio
engineering:hard to build a filter that only works one way
attunement:very_hard to listen on that line and know who's talking
science:hard to find out how a lunch tin is reaching the song
deception:hard to write a letter as someone's dead mother
composure:moderate to answer Ife's second question
fights: choir_drone scouts if the channel stays open too long and something follows it
outcomes: Signed: the letters come through, thousands of words, every one of them true to the people who wrote them. Fourteen children get what no one else in the fleet has got. Within two days a Choir scout is in the next system. It may be a coincidence.
Radio destroyed: the kids stop talking to anybody for a while. Ife brings back the slip, unsigned, and puts it on the captain's desk. Every so often it's there again.
Filter built: letters come in and nothing goes out, in theory. Seven and Aduro read every word. It's the best window on the song anyone has had, and the kids aren't told that.
Used: with the kids' unknowing help, someone asks the song questions. The answers are real. The captain should have to look at Ife every time they use it.
Whatever happens, what the captain says to Ife's second question gets around. She repeats it to everyone she meets, and it's on Garrick Fenn's channel by the end of the week.
gm.rewards: A crayon drawing on the captain's wall, a clue about what the song holds and why it can't hold on, and the respect or the fury of every parent on the Wintermere.
